chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from some of his companions, from Abu Hamza, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

God, Blessed and Exalted, said: 'There is no servant whom I afflict with an affliction and he does not complain to his visitors, except that I replace him with flesh better than his flesh and blood better than his blood. So if I take him (in death), I take him to My mercy; and if he lives, he lives and there is no sin for him.'

key_terms.أَبْدَلَ: To replace/exchange — here God replaces the patient person's body with something better
key_terms.بَلَاء: Affliction, trial — divine testing through illness or hardship
key_terms.ذَنْب: Sin, guilt — the hadith promises the patient person will have no remaining sins
key_terms.عُوَّاد: Visitors to the sick — those who come to visit an ill person (from the custom of 'iyada)
key_terms.قَبَضَ: To seize, to take (in death) — used for God's act of causing death

ai.seo_question: What does Islam say about patience during illness and complaining to visitors?
ai.summary: This is a Divine Hadith (hadith qudsi) narrated through Imam al-Baqir (AS), in which God promises a twofold reward for the patient sick person who does not lament their illness to visitors: bodily renewal in this life (better flesh and blood) and spiritual purification (death unto divine mercy, or complete forgiveness). The hadith addresses 7th-century Shia Muslims in Kufa and Medina, encouraging dignified restraint during illness rather than public complaint, which was considered a form of ingratitude. The phrase 'visitors' (عوّاد) refers to the Islamic custom of visiting the sick (ziyarat al-marid).
